objectives: Recount the foundational milestones of public health from Snow + Chadwick to WHO.
Distinguish primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention with worked examples.
Apply Rose's prevention paradox + Marmot's social gradient to intervention design.

slides.title: The founders: from miasma to germ theory
slides.body:
**Public health** is the science + art of preventing disease, prolonging life, and promoting health through organized efforts of society (Winslow 1920; revisited by Acheson 1988). Distinguishing feature: the unit of analysis is the **population**, not the individual patient.

**John Snow (1813-1858)** — Broad Street pump 1854. London cholera outbreak in Soho; Snow mapped 578 deaths around the Broad Street water pump + showed they clustered in households drawing water from that pump. Removing the pump handle ended the outbreak. Snow's 'Grand Experiment' (comparing Southwark + Vauxhall vs Lambeth water companies) showed cholera rates 14× higher in households served by sewage-contaminated water. Foundational because: (1) waterborne transmission, decades before germ theory; (2) spatial epidemiology + the dot map; (3) natural experiment with comparison groups. Snow's monograph 'On the Mode of Communication of Cholera' (1855) is the founding text of modern epidemiology.

**Edwin Chadwick (1800-1890)** — Sanitary Report 1842. 'Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population of Great Britain' showed that working-class mortality (life expectancy ~22 yr in Manchester slums) was driven by overcrowding + filth, not moral failure. Drove the Public Health Act 1848 (UK), establishing local Boards of Health, sewers, clean water. Inspired similar reforms across Europe + US.

**Lemuel Shattuck (1793-1859)** — Massachusetts Sanitary Commission Report 1850. First systematic American public-health plan: vital statistics, sanitary surveys, smallpox vaccination, school health, occupational health, town health boards. 50 yr ahead of widespread implementation. Foundation of US state public-health departments.

**Louis Pasteur (1822-1895) + Robert Koch (1843-1910)** — germ theory. Pasteur's swan-neck flasks (1859) refuted spontaneous generation; pasteurization (1864) reduced milk-borne disease; rabies vaccine (1885). Koch's postulates (1884) formalized the criterion linking microbe → disease (anthrax 1876, TB 1882, cholera 1883). Together they reframed disease as caused by specific organisms — replacing miasma theory with the germ theory.

**William Farr (1807-1883)** — vital statistics + General Register Office. Built the statistical infrastructure for measuring mortality + understanding epidemics. Farr's law (epidemic curves rise + fall ~symmetrically) preceded SIR modeling.

**Florence Nightingale (1820-1910)** — Crimean War + Coxcomb diagrams. Used data visualization (polar area charts) to show that British soldier deaths in the Crimean War were dominated by preventable disease — driving sanitary reform in military medicine + the founding of evidence-based nursing.

**WHO (1948)** — founded after WWII; Constitution defines health as 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.' Initial focus: malaria, TB, maternal-child health, sanitation. UNICEF (1946), FAO (1945), World Bank health work followed.

**Alma-Ata 1978** — International Conference on Primary Health Care (Halfdan Mahler WHO + UNICEF Grant). 'Health for All by 2000' slogan. Declared primary health care (PHC) the route to equitable health: community-based, intersectoral, affordable, locally appropriate. Tension with **selective PHC** (Walsh + Warren 1979: GOBI — growth monitoring, ORS, breastfeeding, immunization). Modern echo: UHC + SDG 3.

slides.title: Modern milestones: smallpox to HIV to HPV
slides.body:
**Smallpox eradication (1980)** — WHO Intensified Smallpox Eradication Programme (1967-1980) under D. A. Henderson + Frank Fenner. Strategy shifted from mass vaccination to **ring vaccination** (Foege): vaccinate contacts of cases. Last natural case: Ali Maow Maalin, Somalia, 1977. Declared eradicated 1980 by 33rd World Health Assembly. Only human disease ever eradicated. Cost: ~$300M over the campaign; ROI: vaccine + treatment costs saved exceed the cost every few months indefinitely. Henderson's book 'Smallpox: The Death of a Disease' (2009) is the definitive account.

**DOTS for TB (Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course)** — WHO-promoted standardized TB control strategy 1994+: case detection by smear microscopy + 6-9 mo standardized 4-drug regimen with directly observed treatment to ensure adherence + prevent MDR-TB. Karel Styblo's earlier Tanzania work was foundational. Scaling reduced TB mortality 45% from 1990-2015. Now extended to MDR-TB regimens (bedaquiline + delamanid) + Stop TB + End TB strategies.

**Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS)** — Mahalanabis + Phillips + Cash (Cholera Research Lab Dhaka, 1968). Glucose-coupled sodium absorption mechanism (Curran + Schultz). Reduced diarrhea mortality from ~5 million/yr in 1980 to <500k/yr now. 'Possibly the most important medical advance of the 20th century' (Lancet 1978). Cost: ~$0.10 per packet. Combined with zinc supplementation (Bhutta + Black) cuts mortality further.

**ACT for malaria (Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy)** — qinghaosu (artemisinin) isolated by Tu Youyou (Nobel 2015) from Artemisia annua, 1972. WHO recommended ACTs as first-line for falciparum malaria 2001. Combined with insecticide-treated bednets + indoor residual spraying + RDTs. Global malaria deaths fell from ~900k in 2000 to ~600k in 2022. Threat: artemisinin resistance in Greater Mekong subregion.

**Antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV** — combination therapy (HAART) Hammer + Carpenter 1996. Mortality reduced 80%+ in treated populations. PEPFAR (2003 Bush), Global Fund (2002), 3 by 5 initiative (WHO 2003). UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets (95% diagnosed, 95% on ART, 95% suppressed). 'Treatment as prevention' (HPTN 052; Cohen 2011): viral suppression → undetectable → untransmittable. 39 million living with HIV (2023); 30 million on ART.

**HPV vaccine (Cervarix, Gardasil)** — quadrivalent (2006) + 9-valent (2014). Australia → 80% coverage → 90% reduction in vaccine-type HPV in young women within a decade (Brotherton + Garland). Modeling (Hall + Brisson 2019) suggests cervical-cancer elimination is feasible. WHO 2020 strategy: 90% HPV vaccination, 70% screening, 90% treatment.

**Other foundational milestones**: fluoridation of water (1945+ Grand Rapids), polio vaccine (Salk 1955 + Sabin 1961), Framingham Heart Study (1948+), DDT + malaria eradication attempt (1955-1969), seat-belt laws (1968+ US), tobacco control + Surgeon General's report 1964 (Luther Terry), MMR vaccine (1971), Helicobacter + ulcers (Marshall + Warren 1982, Nobel 2005), Folic acid for NTDs (Smithells + Wald 1991+), tobacco MPOWER + FCTC (2003+ first WHO treaty).

slides.title: Key concepts: population thinking, prevention, the social gradient
slides.body:
**Population vs individual perspective** — clinical medicine treats the patient in front of you; public health treats the population. **Geoffrey Rose** (1926-1993; 'Sick Individuals and Sick Populations' 1985) distilled the difference: the determinants of *who in a population gets sick* differ from determinants of *why the population has the rate it does*. Genetic + behavioral variation explain individual cases; population norms (diet, salt, alcohol, smoking, pollution) explain population rates.

**Three levels of prevention** (Leavell + Clark 1958):
- **Primary prevention**: prevent the disease occurring (immunization, sanitation, tobacco control, helmets, fluoridation, prenatal folate). Acts before pathogenesis. Largest population impact.
- **Secondary prevention**: detect + treat disease early, before symptoms (cervical Pap screening, mammography, blood pressure screening, HIV testing, neonatal heel-prick). Acts in pre-clinical phase.
- **Tertiary prevention**: reduce complications + improve quality of life in established disease (cardiac rehab, diabetes care, palliative care). Acts in clinical phase.

Additional category: **primordial prevention** (Strasser + Toharyan 1978) — prevent emergence of risk factors themselves (urban planning for walkability, food-policy reform).

**Rose's prevention paradox** — a preventive measure that brings large benefit to the community offers little benefit to each participating individual. Example: lowering population mean blood pressure 2 mmHg via reduced dietary salt prevents thousands of strokes — but any single individual's risk reduction is small + unmeasurable. Conversely, the **high-risk strategy** (treat those with BP >160) gives large per-person benefit but misses most strokes (which occur in the moderate-risk majority). Most population health gains come from **population shifts**, not individual high-risk targeting alone. Both strategies are typically needed.

**Marmot's social gradient** — Sir Michael Marmot's Whitehall studies (Whitehall I 1967+; Whitehall II 1985+) on British civil servants showed a clean linear gradient: each step down in employment grade was associated with worse cardiovascular + all-cause mortality, even among employed, non-poor adults. **Health is not a poverty problem only** — the gradient runs across the entire social hierarchy. Mechanisms include chronic stress, control + autonomy at work (Karasek + Theorell), social participation, early-life conditions. Marmot's Commission on Social Determinants of Health (CSDH 2008) framed health equity as a global imperative + drove the **social determinants of health (SDOH)** agenda.

**Dahlgren-Whitehead rainbow** — concentric layers of determinants: individual (age/sex/genes) → lifestyle → community + social networks → living + working conditions → general socioeconomic + cultural + environmental conditions. Useful for intervention mapping.

**Health equity vs equality** — equality = equal resources; equity = resources proportional to need. Concept central to modern public-health practice (CSDH; Braveman; Bhutta).

**The 10 Essential Public Health Services** (US, 1994; revised 2020): assess, investigate, communicate, mobilize, strengthen partnerships, create policies, enforce, link to care, ensure competent workforce, evaluate + research, build organizational infrastructure. Frame for state + local PH agencies.

**The Ten Great Public Health Achievements** (CDC 1999): vaccination, motor-vehicle safety, workplace safety, infectious disease control, decline in CHD + stroke, safer + healthier foods, healthier mothers + babies, family planning, fluoridation, tobacco control. Together added ~25 years to US life expectancy in the 20th century (vs ~5 years from clinical medicine alone).

question.question: Reason through Rose's prevention paradox for population blood pressure
question.goal: Population mean SBP is 130 mmHg; SD ~20. Stroke risk rises continuously with BP. A policy lowers mean SBP by 2 mmHg via reduced salt. Reason about who benefits + by how much, vs treating only the high-BP (≥160) subgroup pharmacologically.

steps.prompt: If stroke risk is continuous in BP, where in the BP distribution are most strokes occurring?

acceptedAnswers: most strokes occur in the moderate-BP majority, not the high-BP tail

steps.reveal: Although per-person risk is highest at SBP ≥160, very few people are there. Most of the population sits at 120-150 with moderate per-person risk. Total events = population × per-person risk; the moderate group contributes the majority of strokes by virtue of its size. This is the classic Rose insight — 'a large number of people exposed to a small risk may generate many more cases than a small number exposed to high risk.'

steps.prompt: What's the effect of shifting mean SBP down 2 mmHg on population stroke incidence?
hints: Each mmHg of SBP ≈ 3-4% relative stroke risk.
steps.reveal: Meta-analyses (Lewington 2002; Ettehad 2016): each 10 mmHg drop in SBP cuts stroke ~25-35%. A 2 mmHg population shift gives ~6-8% population-wide reduction in stroke incidence — translating to many thousands of strokes prevented annually in a country of 100M+ adults. Population-wide salt-reduction policies (UK 2003-2011 voluntary reformulation: mean SBP fell ~3 mmHg) realized exactly this benefit.

steps.prompt: What's the per-person benefit to a typical individual in that policy?
hints: Individual absolute risk × policy-induced relative reduction.
steps.reveal: For an individual at average risk (~0.5%/yr stroke), a 6-8% relative reduction means ~0.03-0.04%/yr absolute risk reduction — far below the noise of personal experience. The paradox: individuals see no perceptible benefit from a policy that prevents thousands of population strokes. This is why population strategies feel impersonal + are politically harder to sustain — and why the high-risk strategy (treat people with SBP ≥160 pharmacologically) feels rewarding to clinicians + patients.

steps.prompt: Why is the high-risk strategy alone insufficient?

acceptedAnswers: most strokes occur outside the high-risk group + screening misses many

steps.reveal: Most strokes occur in the moderate-BP majority outside the 'high-risk' tail. Even if every high-BP person were perfectly treated, the majority of strokes would remain. Plus: identifying + treating high-BP requires sustained screening + adherence (often <50% controlled in real populations); population shifts via salt-reduction, sugar tax, tobacco control, alcohol pricing, food reformulation are passive (you don't need to enroll people). Most modern PH practice combines both — but the population strategy is the dominant lever for population-scale outcomes.

acceptedAnswers: BP + risk follow socioeconomic position; upstream policies reduce gradient

hints: Why is BP higher in lower-SES groups?
steps.reveal: Lower SES correlates with higher salt + worse diet + chronic stress + less access to care + worse BP control — yielding the Marmot gradient in stroke + CHD mortality. Population-level food-policy + structural interventions reduce health inequities by acting on upstream causes; the high-risk medical strategy alone tends to widen disparities (better-off comply more with treatment). Rose's strategy + Marmot's equity lens together motivate structural primary + primordial prevention. The CSDH (2008) made this explicit: 'social injustice is killing on a grand scale.'

question.question: Which is the best example of *primordial* prevention?
options: Treating an existing diabetic patient with insulin to prevent complications.
Mass screening adults with fasting glucose to detect prediabetes early.
Designing walkable urban neighborhoods + restricting fast-food advertising to children, so obesity + type 2 diabetes risk factors fail to emerge in the population.
Vaccinating adolescents against HPV to prevent cervical cancer.
question.explanation:
**Primordial prevention** (Strasser + Toharyan 1978) — prevent the *emergence of risk factors themselves*. Walkability, food-policy, advertising restrictions, sugar tax, tobacco price + plain-packaging, lead-paint bans — these act on the social + environmental determinants so that risk factors (obesity, sedentary lifestyle, tobacco use) never develop at population scale.

**Primary prevention** (the other options 'feel' primary): vaccination (HPV → cervical cancer) acts on disease onset, so it is primary prevention; **secondary prevention** screens for asymptomatic disease (prediabetes detection); **tertiary prevention** treats established disease to reduce complications (insulin for diabetes). The distinction matters because primordial prevention has the largest + most equitable population impact, but requires intersectoral action (urban planning, agriculture, education, taxation, trade) — not just the health sector. Rose's + Marmot's frameworks point in this direction. WHO Health in All Policies (HiAP, Adelaide 1988+, Helsinki 2013) operationalizes it.

hints: Primordial = prevent the *risk factor* from arising.
Vaccination prevents disease, not the risk factor.
slides.workedSolution: Primordial prevention acts upstream of risk-factor emergence. Walkable cities + food-advertising restrictions prevent obesity + sedentary behavior from developing → diabetes never emerges. Vaccination is primary prevention (acts on disease). Screening is secondary. Insulin is tertiary.

question.question: Designing a national salt-reduction policy with Rose + Marmot in mind
question.prompt: You are a Ministry of Health advisor in a country with mean adult SBP 134 mmHg + a stroke incidence of 200 per 100,000 PY. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death + lower-SES groups bear 2× the stroke mortality. You have a budget of ~$50M/yr for population CVD prevention. Discuss: (a) what mix of population-wide vs high-risk strategies you would recommend (food-industry reformulation, salt + sugar taxes, labeling, free hypertension screening + medication, urban walkability); (b) how Rose's prevention paradox + Marmot's social gradient inform the mix; (c) what indicators you would monitor + over what horizon to detect impact; (d) intersectoral partners (agriculture, finance, trade, education, urban planning, media) + political-economy obstacles you expect from the food industry; (e) how to address the equity gap explicitly so that the population intervention doesn't widen disparities.

question.question: A country of 50 million adults reduces mean SBP by 2 mmHg through salt-reduction policy. Each 1 mmHg drop in SBP reduces population stroke incidence by ~3%. Baseline stroke incidence is 200 per 100,000 PY. How many strokes are prevented per year?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how John Snow's 1854 Broad Street investigation + Edwin Chadwick's 1842 Sanitary Report + the 1978 Alma-Ata declaration together established the conceptual foundations of modern public health.
question.rubric: Mentions: Snow (1854) — natural experiment + spatial epidemiology + waterborne transmission (before germ theory) + population-level intervention (pump handle); Chadwick (1842) — sanitation as a social + structural determinant of mortality + intersectoral reform via the 1848 Public Health Act; Alma-Ata (1978) — primary health care + 'Health for All' + intersectoral, equitable, community-based approach; together they introduce (a) population thinking, (b) structural / upstream determinants beyond individual behavior, (c) the role of policy + government in disease prevention, (d) equity as a core value. Notes that these foundations resurface in Rose's prevention paradox, Marmot's social gradient, the WHO Triple Billion + UN SDGs. Concludes: modern public health is about populations, structural causes, and equity — not just medicine at scale.
